newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin swaps salvoes with former aide Korzhakov.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin swaps salvoes with former aide Korzhakov.

text.p: A new war of words erupted on Friday between Boris Yeltsin and his former bodyguard and confidant, Alexander Korzhakov -- this time over accusations that the Russian president had tried to commit suicide.

The British newspaper The Guardian quoted Korzhakov as saying that Yeltsin, now 66, suffered from bouts of chronic depression and that he had tried to end his life at least twice, although the attempts stopped two years ago.
The Kremlin hit back with a statement which sought to dismiss Korzhakov as an embittered ex-employee but did not directly address his allegations.

The Kremlin press service said it was not worth getting into an argument with Korzhakov, who was sacked last year after a decade at Yeltsin's side and lost a legal battle against his former boss earlier this month.
"It is senseless starting an argument with a man who is blinded by hurt and motivated in his attitude to the president just by a feeling of revenge," the statement said.

"The former head of the special (bodyguard) service and now a deputy, has not only again crossed the limit of written and unwritten norms of state ethics but has also shown that the concepts of male honour are just an empty noise for him."
The statement did not directly address the accusations by Korzhakov, who is now a member of the lower house of parliament, that Yeltsin had tried to kill himself.

But it dismissed suggestions by Korzhakov, 47, that the Kremlin leader was unable to understand recent international treaties he has signed and said the former bodyguard's other statements were equally suspect.
"What value have Mr Korzhakov's statements that the president allegedly finds it difficult to orient himself in foreign policy matters?" the Kremlin statement said.
"The results of the president's activity in foreign policy and his personal diplomacy in the last half a year alone have had a big effect."

The Kremlin referred directly to last weekend's summit of the Group of Seven industrial nations at which Russia played a bigger role than previously, despite not being a member, and to the signing of a partnership deal with NATO in Paris last month.
"A. Korzhakov's other statements are equally 'reliable'," the statement said.

Yeltsin has portrayed the Paris deal and the G7 summit in Denver as personal successes just months after returning to the Kremlin following almost eight months away with heart trouble and then pneumonia.
Yeltsin has reaffirmed his grip on power since his comeback, but he has looked thin and unexpectedly missed a late-night gala concert during the G7 summit. Aides said he was tired.

Korzhakov, who rose to the rank of general in the KGB security police, became a fierce political opponent after Yeltsin sacked him in a scandal over campaign funding on the eve of last year's presidential election.
Korzhakov alleged that Yeltsin had made comments "damaging to his honour and dignity" when he was dismissed from office but the Supreme Court rejected his case against the president.
